description: Encrypted and enveloped COSE structures: COSE_Encrypt0 (tag 16), COSE_Encrypt (tag 96) and COSE_Mac (tag 97), with AES-GCM or ChaCha20/Poly1305, AES key wrap and the direct recipient algorithm. Two cases carry a Partial IV (label 6), which neither implementation reads and which RFC 9052 Section 3.1 forbids beside an IV; they are the only cases here whose message has to be refused by whoever opens it rather than opened, and the class of each says who is held to that. Where a case carries expectedMessage, the complete message the COSE working group published is the judge, and that pins more than the cryptography: the order of the recipients and the order of the keys in every unprotected bucket. A red row there can mean that a spelling changed rather than that a cipher broke — the Enc_structure and ciphertext checks beside it say which. Each case is produced by both implementations and then handed to the other one to open. Everything here is deterministic once the content key and the nonce are given, and the vectors give both — a generated nonce would make the bytes incomparable, and a generated content key would too. That is the same departure from 'default settings' the signing suite makes, for the same reason. Note what a passing case does NOT establish: an encrypted or MACed message says nothing about who sent it. RFC 9052 Section 8.3 calls it 'either no or very limited data origination', and with more than one recipient there is none at all, because they all hold the same content key. The metrological record is signed for exactly that reason; the case carrying a reading here is a demonstration of cost. Every key is printed in this file and secures nothing.

cases.description: The plain case: AES-GCM with a 128-bit key, algorithm in the protected bucket, nonce in the unprotected one. The Enc_structure it authenticates has THREE elements and no payload — the payload is what gets encrypted, not what gets authenticated alongside — and the 16-byte tag is appended to the ciphertext rather than given a field of its own. Both are places an implementation can be internally consistent and interoperate with nothing.
The same with a 192-bit key. A128GCM and A192GCM are one cipher and two registered identifiers, so a key of the wrong width is not a different strength but a different algorithm.

ChaCha20/Poly1305 (algorithm 24), the COSE working group's chacha-poly-enc-01. It is there for hardware without AES instructions — a charging-station controller often has none, and a software AES there is slow or leaks its key through cache timing — and EVQI Transport §7.2 names it beside AES-GCM as the content encryption for messages that need confidentiality. Within COSE it is shaped like A256GCM on purpose: one 256-bit key, a 96-bit nonce, the 16-byte tag appended, the same three-element Enc_structure. That is exactly why the published message is the judge here and not only the agreement: two implementations that both quietly ran AES-GCM under the name 24 would agree with each other perfectly.

Externally supplied additional authenticated data, which is covered by the AEAD tag without travelling in the message. It goes into the third element of the Enc_structure, so a recipient who does not supply the same bytes cannot decrypt at all — the message does not merely fail an integrity check afterwards.
A detached ciphertext: the message carries nil and the recipient has to be handed the ciphertext separately. The bytes are the same either way, because the Enc_structure never mentions the payload.
CBOR tag 16 is not covered by the AEAD tag, so the untagged message must carry the very same ciphertext as the tagged one.

A tag-44252 reading encrypted rather than signed, which is the arrangement to think twice about. The recipient learns that whoever holds the key wrote it, and cannot show that to anybody else; a customer cannot check the reading without being able to forge one. What encryption genuinely buys here is confidentiality of consumption data on the wire, and the honest arrangement is a signed reading inside an encrypted envelope rather than an encrypted one instead.

A Partial IV (label 6) in the unprotected bucket beside the IV, which RFC 9052 Section 3.1 forbids in so many words: the Initialization Vector and Partial Initialization Vector header parameters MUST NOT both be present in the same security layer. Neither implementation reads label 6 — both carry the name and neither has a reader, and neither has any way to be given the Context IV that a Partial IV is XORed into — so both open this message by its IV and ignore the rest. That is what the row records. It is survey and not normative because the sentence binds whoever builds the message and no sentence found in RFC 9052 binds the receiver to police it: where the document wanted both sides bound it said so, as Section 9 does for a label used twice in one map — MUST NOT generate, and MUST NOT parse and process. Requiring the refusal is therefore a decision about published behaviour rather than a reading of the specification, which is the maintainer's to take, exactly as the eight DER rows of FINDINGS Section 25 were. The row below needs this one: the two messages differ by the crit entry and nothing else.
cases.reason: RFC 9052 Section 3.1: the Initialization Vector and Partial Initialization Vector header parameters MUST NOT both be present in the same security layer

cases.description: The same message with crit [6] in the protected bucket. RFC 9052 Section 3.1 requires that a label listed in crit be processed, and requires the crit and the labels it names to be in the protected bucket; this message meets both, so what it is refused for is the demand itself and not a malformed crit. Neither implementation processes a Partial IV, so for both of them refusing is what the section prescribes rather than what it prefers — the same sentence the x5bag and x5u crit rows of FINDINGS Section 26 rest on, asked of a third registered label that both can name and neither reads. The row above is this message minus the crit entry and both implementations open it, which is what makes the refusal here the crit entry's and nothing else in the message. The Partial IV value is the one RFC 9052 Appendix C.4.2 prints, which is as much of that example as this suite can use: it encrypts with AES-CCM, an algorithm neither implementation offers.
cases.reason: crit names label 6 and neither implementation processes a Partial IV, and RFC 9052 Section 3.1 gives a recipient that cannot process a critical header nothing to do but refuse

cases.description: COSE_Encrypt with one direct recipient, which is COSE_Encrypt0 with ceremony: the recipient structure carries an empty protected bucket, an empty ciphertext and a key identifier, and nothing else. The one visible difference in the body is the context string of the Enc_structure — 'Encrypt' rather than 'Encrypt0' — which is why the two messages have different ciphertexts for the same key, nonce and payload.

The working group's chacha-poly-01: ChaCha20/Poly1305 inside a COSE_Encrypt with one direct recipient whose key identifier is 'sec-256'. Same key as the Encrypt0 case and a different nonce, and the context string of the Enc_structure is 'Encrypt' — so the ciphertexts differ for two reasons at once, and each would suffice. The published message also fixes the recipient's unprotected bucket as algorithm first, key identifier second.

The content key delivered by AES key wrap under a 256-bit key-encryption key. Note that the algorithm follows the width of the KEY-ENCRYPTION key and not of the key being wrapped: A256KW wraps a 128-bit content key perfectly well, and this case does exactly that. AES key wrap is also deterministic — no nonce, no salt — which is safe only because what it wraps is a uniformly random key rather than a message.

The middle AES width of the key-wrap family, which the registry recommends and which had no vector anywhere: A192KW wrapping the same 128-bit content key A256KW wraps above, under the first 24 bytes of that same key-encryption key. The 192-bit width is where a key schedule written for 128 and 256 bits goes wrong — AES-192 runs twelve rounds against ten and fourteen — and while encrypt0-a192gcm already drives that schedule for encryption, key wrap reaches the primitive with no nonce and no tag of its own.

One content key, two recipients, two different key widths. This is what a recipient list is for — and what it costs: both parties hold the same content key afterwards, so the AEAD's integrity guarantee stops distinguishing them. Either of them can produce a message the other will accept as coming from the sender.

COSE_Mac with one direct recipient, which is COSE_Mac0 with ceremony — and the reason COSE_Mac0 exists at all. The MAC_structure differs from a COSE_Mac0's in exactly one string: 'MAC' where the other says 'MAC0'. The tags therefore differ for the same key and payload, which is a check that both implementations use the right one.

The shape of RFC 9052 Appendix C.5.4's second recipient: HMAC 256/256 over a content key wrapped with A256KW. The RFC prints the wrapped key and the resulting tag, and both implementations reproduce them — which pins the key wrap, the recipient structure, the 'MAC' context and HMAC in one chain. The content key here is the one the RFC's wrapped bytes unwrap to.

One content key, two recipients — and the point at which a tag stops meaning anything about origin. A COSE_Mac0 between two parties at least tells each of them that the other made it, on the grounds that they did not make it themselves. This tells nobody that, and RFC 9052 Section 8.2 says so: a MAC 'cannot be used to prove the identity of the sender to a third party'.
